primitives.name: Equilibrium Interest Ratio
primitives.verbatim_quote: The equilibrium ratio of the annual value income yielded by the capital goods created to the present value sacrificed in creating them — that ratio at which no further net conversion (saving and investment) takes place — is the theoretical long-time rate of interest.

primitives.assumptions: Static capital structure, constant returns to scale, perfect foresight.

layer2.mapping: GSI: Bayesian posterior on r^*; GSE: state transition to new capital stock.

primitives.name: Dynamic Capital Supply
primitives.verbatim_quote: As investment takes place, the new income derived from it makes the saving of any given amount constantly easier, thus progressively changing the conditions of supply of new capital.
primitives.assumptions: Investment generates income, increasing marginal utility of saving.

reasoning_traces.think:
The equilibrium interest ratio defines a steady-state condition where capital income equals sacrifice, implying a fixed point in the capital accumulation process. This is modeled via a ratio \dot{K}/K_0 = r^*. The tendency toward equilibrium implies convergence dynamics, expressed as \lim_{t \to \infty} r(t) \to r^*, suggesting a stable attractor in interest rate behavior. However, this assumes constant conditions, which fail under uncertainty. Dynamic capital supply introduces feedback through \frac{dS}{dt} = f(I(t), \eta(S)), where investment increases savings ease, altering capital availability. These primitives form a triadic system: equilibrium rate, convergence tendency, and dynamic supply—each dependent on the others but subject to exogenous shocks. Failure modes include non-convergence due to external disturbances or misalignment between \dot{K} and K_0. The system's robustness depends on bounded perturbations and consistent utility functions.
